observations: All three source tasks ask for the number of distinct values obtainable by fully parenthesizing a fixed sequence of operands and binary operators (+,-,*), preserving order.

The mathematical object is the set of results over all binary parenthesizations of an expression with n operands and n-1 operators; this is exactly interval dynamic programming over sets of achievable values.
The number of full parenthesizations is Catalan(n-1), but the requested quantity is the cardinality of the union of resulting values, so duplicates must be merged.
Failures show two recurring errors: (a) enumerating or estimating instead of computing the exact set, and (b) truncation from manual enumeration; both are avoided by a deterministic set-based DP.
The interface fixes operands and operators with len(operators)=len(operands)-1, so the procedure is well-defined for any valid parameter instance.
procedure_plan: Let operands a[0..n-1] and operators op[0..n-2], where op[k] sits between a[k] and a[k+1]. Define dp[i][j] as the set of all integer values obtainable by fully parenthesizing the subexpression a[i..j]. Base: dp[i][i]={a[i]}. For length L=2..n, for each i with j=i+L-1, initialize dp[i][j]=empty set; for each split k from i to j-1, combine every x in dp[i][k] with every y in dp[k+1][j] using op[k] (+,-,*), inserting x+y, x-y, or x*y into dp[i][j]. Use a set (or hash set) at each interval to deduplicate. Return the cardinality of dp[0][n-1]. Handle n=1 by returning 1 (the single operand). This directly computes the exact number of distinct values; no Catalan enumeration or manual listing is needed.
uncertainty: The procedure is standard and exact for the stated quantity. Residual uncertainty is only about whether the grader expects the count for the exact given operand/operator sequences (it does per the interface); no semantic ambiguity remains. Complexity is exponential in the worst case because value sets can grow, but for the supplied sizes (n<=8, operands in [-10,20]) it is feasible with set-based DP.
